title: Diorbhail says her own line before she can tie a shoe
summary: A child of Tobar dhìreach not yet three years old says her line back four generations at her mother's fire, for the pleasure of the saying and not because she is asked, and the households of Na Glinn Àrda begin to remark on her the way a valley remarks on any child who does an ordinary thing early.

title: Somhairle first sits Diorbhail by the slab
summary: Somhairle takes the seven-year-old Diorbhail up to the slab for a morning, on no more of an asking than that her mother has no need of her, and gives her the small tellings that ring the Line rather than the Line itself, holding that a thing given too soon to too young a head is given badly.

title: A basket-weavers' boy tries the slab and turns back to his creels
summary: A cousin of Diorbhail's goes up to the slab with her twice out of curiosity and finds he can make no sense of the names, choosing to learn the weaving of a creel that holds water instead. Neither thinks less of the other, and it stands as one more fact of the valleys: that the slab takes some and lets others alone.

title: Diorbhail catches a gap between two tellings
summary: Testing her own memory against a household's telling of itself at the ordinary fires, Diorbhail finds a name kept differently from the way the Line keeps it and brings both versions to Somhairle rather than choose between them, and he settles which telling holds truer and tells her the reason for it.

title: Somhairle says at the fire he may not sit many more Samhains
summary: At a Samhain fire before the whole round of the watch-households, Somhairle says plainly that he does not know how many more such nights he will sit among them, and the gathering falls silent around him, having never before heard him say such a thing of himself.

title: Somhairle gives Diorbhail the Line of the Mason whole
summary: Over a single night at the watch-fire, with Beathan's son sitting the turn beside them, Somhairle says the whole Line of the Mason through twice without a name out of place, the same way it was given to him and to Beathan before her, and sets her own name at its foot when he is done.

title: The valleys turn to Diorbhail's fire before Somhairle's
summary: After the giving, households of Na Glinn Àrda begin bringing their children's names to Diorbhail's fire rather than Somhairle's, the way a valley turns by degrees from an old well to a new one dug beside it, the old well no less good for the turning.

title: Somhairle's face is likened to a withered apple
summary: An old woman of the watch-households, seeing Somhairle at a distance one Bealltainn, says he has come to look like a withered apple left too long on the sill. The saying travels the valleys and sticks to him, so that in time the households speak of him by it as easily as by his own name.

title: Somhairle asks Diorbhail what waits for a man with no hall
summary: At a fire with no one else near enough to hear, Somhairle tells Diorbhail the one thing his own father never told him: that he does not know what waits for one of the grove's blood who took no wife of the king's giving and no share of the kingdom, having no hall to be carried into when his years run out.

title: Beathan's son clears the path for Somhairle's stick
summary: In Somhairle's last seasons, Beathan's son walks up before each Samhain to clear fallen branches from the path so the old man's stick will not catch in the dark, and sits longer at the slab on the nights Somhairle climbs to it, though no household asks this of him.

title: Beathan's son finds Somhairle dead against the slab
summary: In the season the valleys keep for turning peat, Beathan's son finds Somhairle sitting against the slab in the grey of a morning, his stick fallen just out of reach, with no mark on him anywhere; word goes down to Dùn ìseal before noon on the fastest pony the round can put under a boy.

title: The king buries Somhairle and keeps a night's vigil
summary: The king comes up on foot the last two miles, buries his son with his own two hands beside the slab, and sits on the turf afterward with his arms round his knees until an old reciter comes to ask, well after dark, whether he will come in to the fire.

title: Beathan's son takes up the whole watch at the slab
summary: With no household troubling to make it formal, Beathan's son takes the watch at the slab as his own to keep entire, as his father had kept it before Somhairle first divided the watching from the reciting between two hands.

title: Diorbhail keeps the Line by mouth and takes no share for it
summary: Diorbhail says the whole Line through twice each Samhain to any of the watch-households who will hear it, adding each year's names to its foot and setting none of it down on leaf or hide, and takes no share from any hall for the keeping, as Somhairle held she must.
